Bank of America's $1.2 billion penalty sends a powerful message to every organization: Ignoring a known compliance problem doesn't make it go away.

The biggest compliance failures often aren't the ones nobody saw coming. They're the ones someone identified, reported, and chose not to fix.

In my latest article, I explore five signs of an effective anti-money laundering compliance program and why real compliance requires more than policies, paperwork, and technology. It requires leadership, accountability, and a culture where people take red flags seriously.

Compliance isn't about having rules. It's about making sure people follow them.

Bank of America knew for years that its monitoring wasn’t escalating potentially suspicious activity to investigators. Almost two years after signing an OCC order to fix it, regulators say the problems persisted.
The result: a penalty of more than $1.21 billion, and over $5 billion in suspicious transactions reported late to FinCEN.
In Part 1 of my series Beyond the Checklist, I break down three lessons from the case:
  1. A monitoring system is only as good as the controls behind it
  2. Customer due diligence doesn’t end at onboarding
  3. Spotting suspicious activity is only half the job
I’m early in my AML/KYC journey, so I’d value your perspective. For those working in this field: when a control weakness is known, what makes it get fixed rather than documented?

#AML #KYC #FinancialCrimeCompliance #TransactionMonitoring #RegulatoryCompliance

Would you hand your house keys to a stranger who promised to “just tidy up”? 🔑
No? Then here’s a plot twist:
Some people are doing exactly that… with their bank accounts. 😅

Big U.S. banks recently noticed something unusual inside customer accounts. 
Not hackers. Not fraudsters.
AI assistants. 
Logging in with the customer’s own username and password.

Bank of America even emailed customers with a polite but firm message: please don’t share your banking password with your AI agent. And if you do, you’re responsible for what it does.

So let’s simplify today’s concept: AI Agents 🤖

Think of AI in two flavours:
💬 The Chatbot = a very smart friend on the phone.
It can tell you which bill to pay. But you still pay it.
🦾 The Agent = a friend with your keys.
It doesn’t just advise. It acts: logs in, clicks buttons, moves money.

That’s a huge leap. Because when an agent acts, three awkward questions pop up:
1️⃣ Who is actually logged in? Some banks can’t easily tell you apart from your AI.
2️⃣ Who said yes? Did you approve that transfer, or did your agent “assume”?
3️⃣ Who pays if it goes wrong? (Spoiler: right now, often you.)

So how are banks responding?

JPMorgan, Citi, Bank of America and Schwab have all drawn a similar line:
👀 AI agents can look (check balances, read statements)
🚫 AI agents can’t move money

Schwab says it’s blocking unauthorised agents more than ten times a week. Jamie Dimon summed up the worry neatly: you don’t want rogue agents, and there could be thousands of them.

My favourite way to picture the banks’ approach is the valet key 🚗
It starts the car and parks it. But it can’t open the glovebox or the boot.
Limited access. Clear boundaries. A human still holds the master key.

The lesson for all of us:
AI agents are coming to finance. That’s not the debate anymore.
The real question is: how much of the key do we hand over, and to whom?

Drop your comments on which AI concept I should untangle next!

Bank of America had resources most community banks will never have, and it still cost $1.2 billion. The seven lessons here scale down: staffing, BSA officer accountability, clean audits, honest lookbacks. Small banks should read this before an examiner teaches it to them.

Bank of America isn't putting $1.9 billion into India just for another fintech opportunity.
It's betting on the scale of India's credit market.

Bank of America has agreed to invest up to Rs.18,268 crore ($1.92 billion) for a stake of up to 49.9% in Jio Financial Service's lending arm, Jio Credit.

What's interesting is how quickly Jio Credit has scaled, crossing Rs.30,667 crore in assets under management within just two years.

But this deal is part of a bigger trend. 

Foreign financial institutions are increasing their bets on India's lending market, with MUFG's investment in Shriram Finance and Emirates NBD's deal with RBL Bank being other examples.

The shift is worth watching. 

Global institutions are looking beyond launching financial products in India. 
They are partnering with businesses that already have local distribution, customer access and the ability to scale.

For Jio, this brings more than capital. 
It also opens access to global expertise in risk management, governance and financial technology.

For founders, there is a bigger takeaway: the next major opportunity may not be another consumer-facing fintech app, but the financial infrastructure that makes credit more accessible and scalable.

Five big US banks now tell customers their AI agent’s losses are theirs. Even after a hack.
 
Citi, PNC and Citizens joined JPMorgan and Bank of America this week. Citi’s terms even cover the case where the agent leaks your login and a criminal uses it.
 
I think the banks are right to draw this line. An agent logging in with your password looks exactly like you. The bank never vetted it, cannot monitor it, and earns nothing for carrying the risk.
 
The gap sits with whoever builds and deploys the agent. When I worked in bank controls, nothing touched customer money without a named owner for the loss.
 
Four questions for any team shipping an agent that touches money or customer data.
 
1. Does it connect through approved APIs, or with the user’s password?
2. Is access scoped, logged and revocable in one step?
3. Can we prove when a user switched it off?
4. If it acts outside its brief, who pays?
 
If the answer to number 4 is “the user”, the product is not ready for a bank account.

Bank of America emailed customers last week asking them not to give their banking password to an AI assistant. It sounds obvious, but it raises a question most of us haven't considered.

AI is moving from answering to acting.
Newer AI tools, called agents, can log into websites, fill in forms and even move money for you. Some ask for your password to do it.

Why that's risky
An AI agent is like a very obedient new employee. It follows instructions without question, including ones hidden on a webpage or in an email it reads for you. If it holds your keys, anyone who fools it does too. And the bank says customers who share logins are responsible for what follows.

A safer setup
Give an app permission for one specific task, which you can cancel anytime, instead of your password.

My take: Before connecting an AI tool to anything important, ask what it could do if tricked.

Bank of America hired 1,000 contractors to fix flaws AI found in its code.
 The finding was the cheap part.
 
They join 3,000 people already working in that area. The flaws were exposed by frontier models including Anthropic’s Mythos.
 
The CEO says the bill is temporary. “Once you patch, you don’t have to patch as much.” 
Technical debt and security are not projects. They are line items, and they need the same diligence every quarter.
 
Engineers who say they’ve worked through these AI scans describe the same picture:
 🔹 Somewhere between a third and 90% of findings turned out to be false positives
 🔹 “Critical” flags landed on internal tools only admins can reach
 🔹 The code was the easy part. Approvals, testing and rollbacks were the bottleneck
 
A model can prove a flaw exists. Fixing it still needs a person who understands the system and signs off on the change. (And compliance always needs a human who is accountable.)
 
Every new model is also a better scanner. The backlog doesn’t drain. It refills.
 
This isn’t only a bank problem. Banks tend to be ahead on security because customer money is at stake. Media is probably more exposed. Old CMS installs with legacy code, header bidding wrappers, dozens of third-party tags, and nothing like 3,000 people on patching.
 
To make the findings actionable, I’d want three things in place:
 ✅ Triage rules that rank findings by real exposure, not scanner severity
 ✅ Remediation capacity in the roadmap, budgeted as a permanent run cost
 ✅ Patch SLAs written into every ad tech and martech vendor contract
 
Security and audit belong on the roadmap as a standing line, not a fire drill.
